conjuncture: At cutoff (2024-07-12), Trump was the presumptive Republican nominee with the nomination formally clinched on March 12, 2024, and recently convicted on 34 felony counts on May 30 — the first US president convicted of a crime. Two opposing forces defined the moment: (a) existential legal jeopardy (pending sentencing originally set for July 11, delayed post-cutoff), which under the incumbent-withdrawal-cascade framework creates near-certain persistence because holding office is a legal necessity; and (b) the dominant political narrative was Biden's potential withdrawal after the June 27 debate disaster, not Trump's. Trump's conviction produced a fundraising surge ($53M in 24 hours) and GOP consolidation rather than defections, consistent with the leadership-persistence-under-threat pattern where external threats harden rather than dislodge a frontrunner. No internal party pressure for Trump to exit existed. The conjuncture was one of asymmetric stability: despite being a convicted felon facing 3 additional pending cases (DC federal, Florida federal, Georgia state), Trump's structural position was the strongest of any point in the campaign — nominated, leading in polling, with a party restructured entirely around his person.

Whether any other trigger could emerge — though the framework strongly predicts persistence under legal jeopardy, the prior-probability-of-trigger framework would note that residual trigger risk (health event, new indictment, party revolt) is never zero over a 4-month horizon to election. In this case, the residual may account for the gap between the framework's ~2-5% and the market's 8% at cutoff
